slides.page_title: The Practice Schema and Sample Data

blocks.text: 1. The Three Tables
Every drill runs on ==three tables==: `departments`, `employees` and `orders`. The data is __small on purpose__, so each result fits on one screen.
2. Foreign Keys

items: `employees.dept_id` → `departments`
`employees.manager_id` → `employees` (self-reference)
`orders.emp_id` → `employees`
The CEO has a **NULL** `manager_id`: the top of the tree

blocks.text: 3. Salary Sample
The **tie** at ==90000== is deliberate: ranking drills show how `RANK` and `DENSE_RANK` treat equal salaries.
4. Why the Traps

items: One employee has a **NULL** `dept_id`
Two rows tie at 90000 salary
Some emails are **duplicated**
Legal has no staff: an empty department
Each trap breaks a naive query

blocks.text: ★ Q42. No orders: NOT EXISTS
**NOT IN** turns UNKNOWN once the list holds a NULL, so every row is dropped. ==NOT EXISTS== only tests whether a row is found.
The employee with a NULL dept_id is excluded: `dept_id = NULL` matches nothing, so AVG is NULL.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Scalar subquery = one value. IN matches a list. EXISTS tests for a match. Prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN when NULLs can appear.

blocks.text: DENSE_RANK solves nth and top-N per group. HAVING finds duplicates, ROW_NUMBER removes them. percentile_cont gives the median. generate_series plus an anti join finds gaps. LAG gives growth.

caption.text:
60 SQL queries to crack any data interview 🎯

Sixty graded drills on PostgreSQL, built on one employees/departments/orders schema. Every task comes with runnable solution code and the exact result it returns on the sample data, so you can check yourself line by line.

The families, in order:

1️⃣ Basics: SELECT, aliases and sorting
2️⃣ Filtering: WHERE, IN, LIKE and NULL
3️⃣ Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, GROUP BY, HAVING
4️⃣ Joins: combining tables
5️⃣ Subqueries: scalar, IN, EXISTS, correlated
6️⃣ Window functions: ranking, LAG and running totals
7️⃣ CTEs: WITH, chaining and recursion
8️⃣ Interview scenarios: the classics

It ends with a one-page SQL drills cheatsheet to revise the night before.

Save this, then work through one family a day.

Comment “sql” to get every query and answer as a PDF.
